waypoints.name: Killen Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Reached on Forest Roads 23, 21 and 2329 from the Randle or Trout Lake side. FR-2329 holds snow well into early summer, so check the road before committing — parties blocked short of the trailhead have had to walk or bushwhack an extra mile or more of road and forest to reach it.

waypoints.name: High Camp Trail Junction
waypoints.directions: Follow Killen Creek Trail #113 up through subalpine forest and meadow for about three miles to the Pacific Crest Trail, and cross straight over onto the High Camp Trail. Killen Creek, crossed low on the trail, is the last dependable running water; everything above is melted snow. The tread thins out above treeline and is easy to lose in the dark or a whiteout, so note landmarks on the way up or carry a track.

waypoints.name: High Camp
waypoints.directions: Another mile on the High Camp Trail ends it at the edge of the Adams Glacier's lateral moraine. Sheltered bivy sites sit slightly higher, in a shallow snow gully just left of the moraine, and more camping is scattered across the benches above that.

waypoints.name: Adams Glacier Base
waypoints.directions: A patchy path runs past the upper camping area and up moraine and snow to the glacier toe, where parties rope up. Judge the timing generously — the volcano's scale flattens distance out and this leg routinely runs two hours. The point of the very early start is to be through the icefall before the sun starts working on it.

waypoints.name: Mount Adams Summit
waypoints.directions: The usual line takes the right-hand side of the glacier for roughly the first two-thirds, threading ice steps and serac lanes, then cuts back left high up onto the unbroken snow of the summit plateau. Which side of the upper icefall goes changes from year to year, and the left-hand option has been found far steeper than the grade suggests — sustained 55 to 65 degrees rather than moderate — so look at it in daylight from below before committing. The crossing beneath the ice cliffs is the stretch to move through fastest, on thin bridges and with backtracking common. Above the icefall the angle eases and two or three false summits stand between you and the true one, so keep navigating rather than trusting the first high point.

waypoints.name: Killen Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Randle, drive south 1 mile on FR 25, bear left onto FR 23 and follow it about 32 miles to FR 2329, signed for Takhlakh Lake Campground. Turn onto FR 2329 and continue about 4.5 miles past Takhlakh Lake to the Killen Creek trailhead; from Trout Lake, FR 23 reaches the same FR 2329 junction in about 24 miles. FR 2329 is gravel and holds snow into early summer. A Northwest Forest Pass and a free self-issued wilderness permit are required.

waypoints.name: High Camp
waypoints.directions: Follow Killen Creek Trail #113 through forest, meadow and huckleberry fields, crossing East Fork Adams Creek (the last dependable water) about 2.5 miles up, to the PCT junction at roughly 6,100 ft. Cross straight over onto High Camp Trail #10 and follow it about another mile to its end on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine, where camps are spread between 7,000 and 7,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (#96)
waypoints.note: Trail 96 begins here on FR 2150; Northwest Forest Pass required and self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of Forest Road 2150, at about 4,600 feet, where the Snowgrass Flat Trail (#96) begins. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and a free self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit is available at the trailhead kiosk. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm current conditions before driving in.

waypoints.name: Snowgrass Flats meadows
waypoints.note: Trail 96 opens into heather meadows and wildflower bogs with reliable creek water; camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself per Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)) — use designated sites above/below the flats instead. Trail 86 splits here toward Goat Lake.

waypoints.name: Trail 97 junction
waypoints.note: Trail 97, the bypass trail, forks west here toward Cispus Basin; stay on Trail 96, which continues up through the meadows to the PCT.

waypoints.name: PCT junction
waypoints.note: Trail 96 tops out on the Pacific Crest Trail; turn north and climb a series of open benches with views of Mt. Adams and the Goat Rocks crest.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy climbers'-path junction
waypoints.note: Unmarked junction where an unmaintained climbers' path leaves the PCT for Old Snowy; many parties stash trekking poles/packs here before the scramble.

waypoints.name: Summit scree/talus scramble
waypoints.note: Final ~0.5 mi/350 ft leaves the tread for loose scree and talus with a short Class 3 hand-climbing section; watch for rockfall dislodged by climbers above and lingering steep snow into early summer.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit (7,880+ ft); panoramic views of Mt. Adams, Mt. Rainier, Mt. St. Helens and the McCall, Conrad and Meade Glaciers, with Packwood Glacier visible just below to the northwest.

waypoints.name: Monument Creek Trailhead (Lost River Road / Harts Pass Road)
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead on Lost River Road (FR 5400 spur); no parking pass needed; fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk. There is no toilet or drinking water here.

waypoints.name: Robinson Pass
waypoints.note: Gains the Middle Fork Pasayten divide via a steep final 1.2-mile forested pitch; trail forks here toward the Pasayten River valley.
waypoints.directions: Trail #478 follows Robinson Creek through big timber for about six miles, never far from the sound of the water, then fords the creek. Above the ford the grade stays gradual through forest, crossing several avalanche runouts, and breaks into meadowland near 4,700 ft. Pass the Slate Pass Trail junction and finish with a half mile of open meadow climbing to the pass.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten River flats
waypoints.note: Common first-night camp beside the river a few miles below Robinson Pass; reliable water but mosquito-heavy in early season.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and descend about three miles into the broad U-shaped Middle Fork valley, losing roughly 1,800 ft to river level. Camps sit along the water here.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.note: Green alpine lake ringed by larches with a popular established camp; last dependable water before the Rolo/Shellrock high country.
waypoints.directions: Continue down-river before the trail turns and climbs back into the high country, gaining around 2,100 ft to the lake basin. Fred's Lake sits a short way off the main trail rather than on it, so watch for the spur or you will walk straight past it.

waypoints.name: Rolo Pass
waypoints.note: Ridge-crest pass just above Fred's Lake; route continues cross-country toward the head of Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin.
waypoints.directions: From the lake keep climbing to the ridge-crest pass a few hundred feet above, through open larch and talus. The maintained tread thins out above the lake, and this is where the route stops being a trail hike.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Pass / Shellrock Basin
waypoints.note: Trail here has been unmaintained for decades and the basin fogs in frequently; easy to lose the faint tread in whiteout, navigate by map/compass.
waypoints.directions: From Rolo Pass drop to the headwaters of Eureka Creek and traverse across into Shellrock Basin, then climb to the pass at 7,500 ft. The tread through here has been unmaintained for decades and is faint to nonexistent, and the basin fogs in readily — carry map and compass and be ready to navigate without seeing any of the surrounding peaks.

waypoints.name: Lost Peak
waypoints.note: Reached along the ridge from Butte Pass and Pass Butte over several false summits; the loose west and southwest slopes are the other way down.
waypoints.directions: From a camp near the pass, gain either the southwest or the northwest ridge and follow it over talus and alpine meadow to the top. Class 3 with no sustained technical ground, but the crest is high, exposed to wind, and can hold snow well past midsummer.

waypoints.name: Andrews Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; trail #504 starts in a 2003-burn zone with little shade for the first several miles.
waypoints.directions: Drive West Chewuch Road / FR-51 north out of Winthrop roughly 22-23 miles to the road end at about 3,050 ft. Everything above is gained on foot — this is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state, and the Chewuch River trailhead to the east is a longer alternative to the same camp.

waypoints.name: Andrews Creek (burn-zone crossings)
waypoints.note: Trail parallels and repeatedly crosses Andrews Creek through the burn — last easy, frequent water before the climb toward the pass.
waypoints.directions: Trail #504 climbs steadily up the Andrews Creek drainage through the 2003 burn scar: little shade, brushy regrowth that soaks you through after rain, and blowdown between trail-crew visits. The creek runs beside the tread for these miles, so there is no reason to carry much water on this stretch.

waypoints.name: Peepsight Trail junction
waypoints.note: Stay on Andrews Creek Trail (left/straight) for Andrews Pass; the right fork climbs to Peepsight Lake.
waypoints.directions: Stay on #504 as it continues up-valley. The Peepsight Trail branches off toward Peepsight Creek and eventually rejoins the Andrews Creek line much higher by a far longer loop — not the way to Cathedral. Burn and brushy tread continue past the fork.

waypoints.name: Andrews Pass
waypoints.note: Burn zone ends and open meadow country begins here; dispersed camps sit on the bluff just east of the pass, trail then contours toward Spanish Creek and the Boundary Trail.
waypoints.directions: Above the Peepsight fork the trail keeps grinding up the drainage in burned timber until it tops out at the pass, where open parkland and meadow replace the snags and the view opens north toward Amphitheater Mountain. Snow patches can hold on this stretch into early July.

waypoints.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp
waypoints.note: Established basecamp used by SE Buttress climbers, in parkland meadows just west of Cathedral Pass; last reliable water before the route.
waypoints.directions: From the pass follow the Boundary Trail (#533) through rolling meadow toward Spanish Creek, then take the Cathedral Lakes side trail, which bears off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin, for the last few miles into the lake basin. Budget a full, long day from the car to here; most parties arrive mid-afternoon.

waypoints.name: Cathedral Pass
waypoints.note: 40-60 min walk from camp; the Pacific Northwest Trail crosses here between Cathedral Peak and Amphitheater Mountain — leave the trail toward the Cathedral-Monk gully.
waypoints.directions: A 40-60 minute walk from camp, climbing east out of the lake basin on the trail that crosses the pass between Cathedral Peak and Amphitheater Mountain. Leave it at the first switchback above the pass and start up toward the gully.

waypoints.name: Cathedral–Monk gully approach
waypoints.note: Loose, wide gully separating Cathedral Peak from The Monk; route starts about 150 ft up it — watch for rockfall from other parties above.
waypoints.directions: Cross meadow and talus toward the obvious deep cleft between Cathedral Peak and the pinnacle called The Monk. There is no climbers' path, so pick the line by eye — 30 to 60 minutes from camp in total. Scramble up into the gully; the first pitch is on the left (north) wall a short way in, launched from a tall pedestal that makes a solid belay stance.

waypoints.name: Cathedral Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit atop the route's two-pitch headwall; descend trending west then southwest, 4th-class with an exposed gap crossing, back down into the meadows above Upper Cathedral Lake.
waypoints.directions: Ten pitches up the buttress: corners, a chockstone and chimney ground low down, easier discontinuous terrain through the middle, then the sustained headwall — linking pitches 8 and 9 into one 55-60 m lead avoids the route's only semi-hanging belay. Two short hand-crack steps and third-class scrambling finish at the true summit.

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large parking lot on SR 20 just east of milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass. The trail follows Canyon Creek about 6 miles to the Mill Creek Trail junction, the start of this route's approach. The east-side line up the East Ridge starts elsewhere, at a locked gate on the Slate Creek road below Harts Pass (about 3,800 ft).
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead just past milepost 141, about 33 miles east of Marblemount or 55 miles west of Winthrop; the large parking area is at about 1,900 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee (self-pay station on site) is required to park.

waypoints.name: Mill Creek ford
waypoints.note: Ford Mill Creek just below the trail junction — last reliable, easy-to-reach water before the long climb toward Azurite.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Canyon Creek trail upstream along Canyon Creek about 5.7 miles to the ford of Mill Creek, the last easy water before the long climb.

waypoints.name: Mill Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Canyon Creek tread here and turn up the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail; maintained trail effectively ends beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: From the ford continue a short way to the junction where the Mill Creek Trail toward Azurite Pass leaves the Canyon Creek trail.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Mill Creek Trail
waypoints.note: Tread disappears under heavy slide alder and downed timber left from the mine-era trail's disuse — expect a slow, scratchy alder-hacking bushwhack for several miles.
waypoints.directions: Turn up the Mill Creek Trail and follow it up the Mill Creek valley. Within a couple of miles the tread begins to vanish under slide alder and downed timber, and the going becomes a slow bushwhack.

waypoints.name: Azurite Mine
waypoints.note: Flat ground amid the old defunct copper/silver mine workings on Mill Creek; the common overnight camp before pushing toward the Ballard basin.

waypoints.name: Azurite–Ballard basin
waypoints.note: Reached via roughly 3 more brush-choked miles above the mine; open basin at the base of Ballard's south slopes and a typical bivy before the summit push.

waypoints.name: South-face brush and gully route-finding
waypoints.note: Steep, loose terrain with several look-alike chutes low on the south face — picking the wrong gully here is the main way parties get cliffed out or turned back.
waypoints.directions: From the basin, push north through the brush band low on the south slopes onto steep, rocky ground, where several look-alike chutes split the face around 7,400 ft. Read the ground before committing to one, and do not follow the clean-looking south ridge, which is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme.

waypoints.name: North Fork Entiat Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-5606; vault toilet, no potable water; Northwest Forest Pass or $5 self-issue day-use fee required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From US-97A at Entiat, turn onto Entiat River Road (County Road 19, which becomes FS Road 51) and drive about 32 miles up the valley, then turn right onto FS Road 5606, about two miles past Silver Falls Campground. Follow FS Road 5606 about 3 miles to its end at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

waypoints.name: Fern Lake Trail #1436 spur junction
waypoints.note: Fern Lake Trail splits left toward the lake; stay right on Trail #1437 continuing up the North Fork Entiat valley.
waypoints.directions: Take North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 upstream on a gentle grade — only about 1,300 ft of gain spread over six miles. The lower miles run through old burn and blowdown, so plan on working over, under and around deadfall rather than walking a clean tread. A creek crossing a few miles in has been made variously on a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail or on a footbridge, so look at what is actually standing rather than counting on either.

waypoints.name: Pyramid Creek / Pyramid Mtn Trail #1433 junction
waypoints.note: Trail forks here; take the upper-left fork signed toward Pyramid Mountain Trail to head into the Emerald–Saska basin rather than continuing up the North Fork.
waypoints.directions: Bear right at the Fern Lake fork and stay on #1437 up the valley. Around mile 7 the trail swings sharply east and switchbacks for about half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail. Early season the tread gets hard to follow once snow patches start above roughly 4,800 ft, so keep track of the valley line rather than the footprints.

waypoints.name: Fox Camp
waypoints.note: Small established camp about a quarter mile past the Pyramid Creek junction; last reliable camp before the climb into the high basin.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the junction and head west; the timber opens into a clearing within about a quarter mile. Fill and treat water here — the valley bottom is the last easy water, and there is little of it once the route climbs into the high basin.

waypoints.name: Emerald-Saska basin camp
waypoints.note: Open larch basin between Emerald and Saska Peaks with a seasonal stream; the standard high camp used to climb both summits.
waypoints.directions: From the clearing the travel is cross-country. Angle west then southwest, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald. Expect to give back 200–300 ft of elevation to skirt cliff bands before regaining the open basin floor.

waypoints.name: ~7,800 ft bench below SE ridge
waypoints.note: Broad bench where several similar-looking scramble lines diverge toward the summit block; bear climbers' right to stay on the standard southeast ridge/gully line.
waypoints.directions: Cross the shoulder above the basin near 7,100 ft and climb the gully system into the upper basin wedged between Saska and Emerald, which feeds the southeast side of the summit ridge. The slabby watercourse draining that basin gives the most continuous line and holds snow well into early summer. Keep climbing to the broad bench under Emerald's southeast face.

waypoints.name: Summit scree gully
waypoints.note: Boot-packed path up a steep scree/loose-rock gully below the final scramble; expect two-steps-forward-one-back footing and rockfall risk from parties above.
waypoints.directions: From the bench several scramble lines look much alike and none is obviously better than the rest; work up and to climbers' right to stay on the standard line. The gully holds moderate snow early in the season, wanting an axe and possibly crampons, and is loose scree once it melts out.

waypoints.name: Emerald Peak summit
waypoints.note: Narrow rocky true summit (8,422 ft); Class 3 exposure on the last few moves, with views down to Lake Chelan roughly 7,000 ft below.
waypoints.directions: The gully tops out at a notch in the summit ridge; from there it is a short Class 2–3 scramble to the top. The rock is blocky and loose and there is real exposure on the last few moves, so keep the party close together rather than stacked in the fall line.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit required at the kiosk; Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee for parking (Cooper Lake Rd / FR-46).
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 80 (Roslyn/Salmon la Sac), turn north on Bullfrog Road for 2.8 miles through two traffic circles, then take SR 903 north through Roslyn and past Cle Elum Lake to the junction with Cooper Lake Road (FR 46), about 16.8 miles from I-90. Turn left on FR 46 for 4.7 miles, then right on FR 4616 for about a mile to the Pete Lake Trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass and a free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit are required.

waypoints.name: PCT junction near Lemah Meadow
waypoints.note: Climbers' bypass leaves the Pete Lake Trail/PCT corridor here near 4,000 ft, cutting the Lemah Meadow dogleg to save ~3 miles.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 up the Cooper River on gentle, mostly flat forest tread about 4.5 miles to Pete Lake, then continue to a fork about five miles in and turn right. After about 0.6 mile, turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail.

waypoints.name: Vista Lakes (upper lake)
waypoints.note: Established high camp at the upper Vista Lake tarn; warm swimming water and the standard bivy for a summit push.
waypoints.directions: Climb the PCT north up its long series of switchbacks for about 4.5 miles to about 5,500 ft. The Vista Lakes tarns lie just east of the trail at that height; this is the last reliable water.

waypoints.name: Point 5965 / Summit Chief Pass
waypoints.note: Climb easy terrain west of Vista Lakes over Pt. 5965, then drop to Summit Chief Pass and pick up the ridge running northwest toward the peak.
waypoints.directions: Leave the PCT and head cross-country west and north-west from the lakes over easy terrain on Vista Ridge, over Point 5965, then drop to Summit Chief Pass.

waypoints.name: Summit Chief Lake talus basin
waypoints.note: Lower talus basin by a snowfield below Summit Chief Lake; common spot to stash packs before the final climb.
waypoints.directions: From the pass follow the ridge north-west, staying below the cliffs and gendarmes and west of Summit Chief Lake, across sloping slabs cut by slots and gullies into the talus basin south-east of the summit. Dropping to about 6,000 ft to take the scree avoids the worst of the slabs.

waypoints.name: Moat / icy entry gully
waypoints.note: A moat here can be trip-ending after mid-July or in low-snow years; the adjoining gully is often icy in the morning, so carry crampons.
waypoints.directions: Climb steep hardpan, talus and the snowfield below the south-east face toward the point where the mountain steepens at about 7,000 ft and a moat forms. Avoid the first, left-most snow finger, which dead-ends in a deep notch; head for the upper right corner of the snowfield.

waypoints.name: Notch in the south ridge skyline
waypoints.note: Small notch gained by a rising talus traverse; this is the turnaround/gear-swap point for the final loose gully to the top.
waypoints.directions: Past the moat, exit onto steep dirt and scree and take a left-slanting ramp up to the small notch in the south ridge skyline.

waypoints.name: Summit Chief Mountain (true summit)
waypoints.note: True summit on the King/Kittitas county line, 9 miles NE of Snoqualmie Pass; descend by reversing the loose upper gully and steep dirt to the ridge notch.
waypoints.directions: Cross the notch into the southwest gully system: a steep gully, often icy in the morning, then loose rock, steep dirt and a slightly outward-dipping slab. Exit by the gully on the right just below the summit.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive to the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road, Forest Road 9737: from I-90 take exit 85 near Cle Elum onto SR 970 heading northeast, then follow the Teanaway River Road roughly 23 miles to the road-end parking at about 4,243 feet. The road is gravel and is not maintained through winter, typically staying snowed in until late June in a heavy year, so check conditions before an early-season trip.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue day-use wilderness permit and NW Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Take Icicle Creek Road to Eightmile Road (FR-7601) and follow it to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and you self-issue a day-use wilderness permit at the kiosk. Worth knowing before you commit to a date: the firm spring snow this route wants, April through June, falls largely before the May 15 to Oct 31 permit season.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and camps; head along the north shore toward the Colchuck Glacier.
waypoints.directions: From the trailhead, follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles to the signed junction, turn left onto Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, cross the creek and switchback up to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft. Camps are along the shore toward the south end.

waypoints.name: North shore / glacier approach
waypoints.note: Ascend easy snow on the Colchuck Glacier's east lobe toward Colchuck Col.
waypoints.directions: Follow the trail along the lake's west shore to the boulder field at the south end, then climb talus and the moraine onto the Colchuck Glacier below the Colchuck-Dragontail col.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Colchuck Peak and Dragontail; the couloir start is a couple hundred feet left (east) of the col.
waypoints.directions: Climb the glacier to Colchuck Col, the saddle between Colchuck Peak and Dragontail. It is mostly snow early in the season and firm neve or ice with talus showing later; carry crampons and an axe, and look for a snow finger on the right if a band of blue ice spans the snowfield.

waypoints.name: Pandora's Box notch
waypoints.note: Steep snow/ice couloir (up to roughly 35-40 degrees near the bottom) leading to a notch in the ridge; some parties rope up here.
waypoints.directions: The couloir entrance is not at the col but a couple hundred feet toward Dragontail along the base of the ridge. Climb the couloir, firm 40-45 degree snow early in the season and loose Class 3 talus by late summer, to the notch that cuts right through the ridge.

waypoints.name: Dragontail Peak summit
waypoints.note: From the notch, drop down and traverse northeast to the true summit; descend via Aasgard Pass.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, descend the steep, narrow snow finger on the far side, or leave the couloir about 30 ft below the notch and climb about 20 ft of Class 4 rock to the ridge. Traverse the easier snow and talus below the south side of the ridge, exposed in places, and scramble up to the summit.

waypoints.name: Aasgard Pass
waypoints.directions: Descend to the saddle southeast of the summit, then make the long traverse east across the snow slope to Aasgard Pass.

waypoints.name: Beverly Turnpike Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-9737-112 off Beverly Creek Road; cross the stout bridge over Beverly Creek right at the trailhead — Northwest Forest Pass required for parking.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road to Beverly Creek Road and follow FR-9737-112 to its end at roughly 3,450-3,600 ft. Wildfire damage has closed this trail system before, so confirm current Forest Service status before committing to the drive in.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek Trail fork
waypoints.note: Beverly Turnpike Trail forks here; leave the Beverly Creek roadbed and turn right (east) up the Bean Creek valley onto Trail #1391.1.
waypoints.directions: Start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed alongside Beverly Creek. At the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the Beverly drainage, which is the wrong valley for this peak.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Bean Creek in a tight, steep valley; can run cold and pushy during June snowmelt, and the trail crosses old avalanche debris just above here.
waypoints.directions: The Bean Creek Trail climbs steadily through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley before dropping to the water. It is an easy rock-hop by mid to late summer, but in May and June snowmelt it runs cold and pushy and is the real decision point of the day; the trail crosses old avalanche debris just above the ford.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek Basin junction
waypoints.note: Trail forks at the edge of subalpine meadows: stay left for Bean Creek Basin's wildflower fields or bear right/east for the Earl Peak saddle approach.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing through forest until it breaks open into the basin — a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. Fill water here. Bean Creek is the last dependable source and there is none above the meadows.

waypoints.name: Earl Pass (southwest ridge gain)
waypoints.note: Saddle on the divide between Bean and Standup Creek drainages; leave the boot path here and gain the southwest ridge toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than continuing left into the upper basin. Tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking up to the broad saddle on the divide, about 2,600 ft of gain in all from the car.

waypoints.name: False summit / loose scree pitch
waypoints.note: Class 1 but exposed to extremely loose, kickable scree on an approximately 70-degree pitch just below the true summit — easy to mistake for the top.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at the pass and pick up the intermittent boot track climbing the ridge directly toward the summit. This is the sustained part of the day: roughly 800 vertical feet of unrelenting class 2 on loose scree, sand and broken rock, with the track fading in and out. Go slowly, test what you stand on, and stay out from under anyone above.

waypoints.name: Earl Peak summit
waypoints.note: Talus/heather summit block with views across the Teanaway to Mount Stuart; a short ridge scramble continues north to Bean Peak for those extending the trip.
waypoints.directions: From the false top the remaining ground is short — a few more minutes of the same loose ridge tread and talus over the last rise, with no harder moves than what you have already done.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River Bridge / FR 38 Gate
waypoints.note: Gated bridge on FR 38 (Dailey Quarry Road) off Mosquito Lake Road; park at the gate even if open; no parking permit is needed, but the private timberland road beyond requires the landowner's fee access permit, and many parties bike it.
waypoints.directions: From WA-542, turn onto Mosquito Lake Road and follow it to FR-38 (the Dailey Quarry Road), then take FR-38 to its end at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, around 1,200 feet. Park at the gate even if you find it open — no permit is required to park here, though the road is closed to vehicles beyond this point and most parties continue from here by mountain bike.

waypoints.name: Dailey Prairie
waypoints.note: Old logging/quarry road passes this open prairie flat (a DNR Natural Area Preserve) before dropping into the basin between the Twin Sisters.
waypoints.directions: Ride or walk the old quarry and logging roads up from the gate. The grade is easy but the network branches repeatedly and the correct fork is rarely the obvious one, so follow a recorded track rather than instinct. Wrong turns here are the most common way to lose time on this route.

waypoints.name: Orsino Creek Crossing
waypoints.note: Last reliable water on the route; climbers' path crosses here and most parties stash bikes at this point before continuing on foot.
waypoints.directions: Past the prairie the roadbed drops into the basin between the two Sisters, taking a succession of left-hand forks as it goes. The road deteriorates until it is too rough or overgrown to ride, usually marked by a large culvert pipe where the timber road ends. Stash bikes in the trees and fill water at the crossing, because this is the last reliable source on the route.

waypoints.name: Orsino Creek Basin / Red Talus Slope
waypoints.note: Brushy old road fades to a boot path through timber then a red talus field opening into the upper basin below the West Ridge; talus often snow-covered into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot heading southeast. It is brushy and wet in places but followable; it drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and simply ends at a red talus slope that often holds snow into midsummer. From the talus traverse up and right (south), over a timbered rib and past the ruins of an old log cabin, into the upper basin.

waypoints.name: West Ridge Notch
waypoints.note: Gain the West Ridge crest here, roughly 1,800 ft below the summit; higher up, from a second notch about 400 ft below the summit, a traverse right (south) leads to easier Class 2-3 gullies instead of the ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: Climb out of the basin on steep dirt, scree and talus toward the obvious low notch in the ridge above. Sight the notch from the basin floor before starting up, and expect poor footing the whole way; this is the least pleasant stretch of the day.

waypoints.name: Dihedral in the upper cliff band
waypoints.note: Prominent dihedral in the cliffy band around 6,500 ft, below the false summit that parties often mistake for the true top; loose, abrasive dunite rock and a couple of low-5th-class moves here if staying on the ridge crest rather than dropping to the south-face gullies.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge up from the notch, roughly two hours of class 2-3 scrambling that moves on and off the crest. The right (south) side is generally solid and the left side is looser, and holding strictly to the crest is harder than dropping slightly south to bypass steps. The dunite is abrasive and holds friction unusually well, but it is hard on hands and rope. The ridge steepens into a cliffy band around 6,500 ft where the large dihedral sits.

waypoints.name: South Twin Sister
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Twin Sisters Range; two USGS benchmark caps and a summit register are on top, with Mount Baker visible 10 miles to the northeast.
waypoints.directions: The first high point above the dihedral is not the top and carries no cairn or register. Continue along the crest a short distance, on the order of fifty yards, crossing talus and any lingering snow to the next high point, which holds the survey markers and the register. In fog this last short stretch is where parties stop short and turn around believing they have summited.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required; parking lot is just past the Downey Creek bridge on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), about 20 mi from Hwy 530.
waypoints.directions: Drive Suiattle River Road (FR 26) about 20 miles in from Highway 530; the parking area sits just past the Downey Creek bridge at roughly 1,450 feet. Display a Northwest Forest Pass. Check the road before you commit to the trip, because it is frequently washed out or gated well short of the trailhead, adding miles of walking or biking each way that none of the trail mileage here accounts for. The route is normally in condition July through September.

waypoints.name: Sixmile Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp along the easy, flat Downey Creek Trail #768 where the route leaves the maintained trail and turns east along Bachelor Creek.
waypoints.directions: Follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles from the trailhead — easy, well-graded and mostly flat through forest, with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford or log-cross Bachelor Creek to its south side here; the climbers' path above is badly overgrown with slide alder up to roughly 4,400 ft.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends here; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first, then ford to the south side at about the 9.5-mile mark. Treat it as a real creek crossing — harder and more dangerous in high water or early season.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake Pass
waypoints.note: Gap on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake (~5,880 ft), gained by switchbacks; begin the ~500 ft descent to the lake basin from here.
waypoints.directions: Climb the climbers' path above the crossing. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone, so expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber; above the debris the path climbs to the pass on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake
waypoints.note: High camp with reliable water at the lake basin; Itswoot Ridge, reached by traversing further, is the alternate camp some parties use instead.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 500 ft off the pass into the lake basin. These are snow slopes into midsummer and this is normally the crux navigation of the approach day when they are covered.

waypoints.name: Dome Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the Dome Glacier's crevasses toward the Dome-Sinister col; a bergschrund spans the glacier and requires finding a solid snowbridge.
waypoints.directions: Most parties push on from the lake basin up onto Itswoot Ridge for high camp, then traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the glacier. Rope up for glacier travel and carry crevasse-rescue gear before starting across.

waypoints.name: Dome-Sinister col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Dome and Sinister Peaks; from here contour on an easy snowfield around to Sinister's south side to reach the loose southwest gully.
waypoints.directions: Cross over the Dome–Chikamin col and descend the crevassed Chikamin Glacier to about 7,200 ft, then traverse right (east) across the glacier to the col. The bergschrund guarding it can be hard to cross in late season and has sometimes required a short rappel to get down onto or across it.

waypoints.name: Sinister Peak
waypoints.note: True summit, just under a mile east of Dome Peak along the connecting ridge; reached via the loose southwest gully to the upper west ridge.
waypoints.directions: From the col contour around on an easy snowfield to Sinister's south side, then climb the loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge and scramble Class 2–3 along the ridge to the top. Loose rock in the gully is the main hazard — move fast and keep the party out of each other's fall line; some parties skip it and take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard, single approach for all Southern Pickets/Terror Basin objectives including Little Mac Spire.
waypoints.directions: From SR-20 at Newhalem, turn north onto the gravel road across the highway from the Newhalem Campground and follow signs toward the Goodell Creek group camp; park at the small turnout at the trailhead just before the camp.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Crossings
waypoints.note: Trail fords two branches of Goodell Creek that run high on hot afternoons; a small streamside campsite sits near the second crossing.
waypoints.directions: Follow the unmaintained but well-trodden climbers' trail north along the old, overgrown logging road bed paralleling Goodell Creek. The walking is forested and comparatively gentle to the creek crossings.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Cairn / Climbers' Path
waypoints.note: Large cairn and stone arrow mark the turn off the maintained Goodell Creek trail onto the steep, faint climbers' path south of Terror Creek — the start of the '~4,000 ft over 2 mi' push.
waypoints.directions: Continue along the old road bed to its end, where a large cairn and stone arrow mark a hard right turn uphill onto the Terror Basin climbers' path.

waypoints.name: Rocky Streambed Source
waypoints.note: Last dependable water on the climbers' path, running in a rocky streambed; the faint tread resumes just upstream.
waypoints.directions: Turn right and climb the path, which goes brutally steeply more or less straight up the timbered ridge nose between Terror and Crescent Creeks, through brush and a class 3 root-pull cliff band, to the rocky streambed where the last dependable water runs.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Notch
waypoints.note: Gap on the east rim of Terror Basin reached via a rising traverse over moderate snow into midsummer; first view down onto the basin and the McMillan/Little Mac group.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the faint tread just upstream and make a rising traverse, over moderate snow into midsummer, to the 6,200 ft gap on the east rim of Terror Basin.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Shared high camp for the whole McMillan/Terror cluster — flat gravel benches, running water, and rock-walled bivy sites; base for Little Mac, East Mac, and West Mac.
waypoints.directions: Drop down the scree or snow on the far side of the notch to the flat gravel benches of camp at about 5,800 ft.

waypoints.name: Loose Rock Below the Summit Block
waypoints.note: Southern Pickets rock is notoriously fractured here; test holds and stagger climbers on the 5.4 pitches to avoid knocking rock onto partners below.

waypoints.name: Little Mac Spire
waypoints.note: Approximate — no independently surveyed summit coordinate found for this minor Southern Pickets spire; cross-referenced against neighboring McMillan/Terror group summits and the route's recorded approach track to place it as close to the true high point as possible.

waypoints.name: Westside Road / Dry Creek (Tahoma Creek) Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of driveable Westside Road (3.2 mi from the Nisqually-Longmire Rd junction), gated at Dry Creek. Check this before you drive: the National Park Service's only two listed accesses to Indian Henry's Hunting Ground — the next waypoint on this route — are Kautz Creek (11.5 mi round trip) and Longmire (13 mi round trip). The Westside Road and Tahoma Creek corridor is not among them, and route beta for Success Cleaver reports the Tahoma Creek Trail closed for flood hazard, leaving Longmire via the Wonderland Trail as the standard approach. The mileages recorded on this route's waypoints are measured from this Dry Creek gate, so they describe the older corridor rather than a Longmire or Kautz Creek start — treat them as approximate if you approach from either of those, and confirm current trail status with a wilderness information centre.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 706 to the Nisqually Entrance in the park's south-west corner; the road is paved and open essentially year round, conditions permitting. Westside Road leaves the Nisqually to Longmire road and is driveable about three miles to the gate at Dry Creek, where a standing, non-seasonal closure caused by repeated Tahoma Creek washouts stops vehicles; past the gate it is open to foot and bike traffic only. Longmire, where the nearest wilderness information centre is and where you register in and out, lies about 3.5 miles further along the main road.

waypoints.name: Indian Henry's Hunting Ground (patrol cabin)
waypoints.note: Historic 1915 patrol cabin marks where the route leaves the maintained Wonderland Trail for cross-country travel toward the Mirror Lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Mirror Lakes
waypoints.note: Small tarns about a mile off the Wonderland Trail; last dependable water before contouring dry southwest/west slopes of Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained Wonderland Trail at the patrol cabin and take the Mirror Lakes spur west, crossing marshy meadow on a series of plank walkways. Maintained tread ends part way along and the path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft, in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak, roughly a mile off the Wonderland. These tarns are the last dependable water before the dry south-west and west slopes of Pyramid Peak.

waypoints.name: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
waypoints.note: Flat campsites just north of this 6,631 ft high point give broad views of Success Cleaver.
waypoints.directions: From the tarns it is cross-country travel. Head north-east out of the basin and contour the south-west then west slopes of Pyramid Peak, staying roughly between 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. There is no boot-pack and only sparse cairning through here, so carry a map or GPS track and expect to find your own line; snowmelt water is often available around the point into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak near 6,300 ft is a common first night.

waypoints.name: 6,400 ft saddle below Success Cleaver
waypoints.note: Short descent NNE from Point 6631 to this saddle; typical high camp before scrambling onto the lower cleaver at first light.
waypoints.directions: Drop north-north-east from Point 6631 a short way to the saddle at about 6,400 ft, which is the start of Success Cleaver proper. It is a scree and loose-boulder col and it looks unpleasant, which is how you know it is the right place. There is an easier way down into it than the obvious line, and parties record missing it and taking the worst ground, so pick the descent out before you commit and note it for the return.

waypoints.name: Lower Success Cleaver gendarmes
waypoints.note: Loose rock towers force weaving route-finding on the lower rib; rockfall risk climbs if other parties are above; bivy options around 8,100-8,300 ft.
waypoints.directions: From the col the cleaver rises straight ahead and does not let up: loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, no track and no cairned line, weaving among rock towers on ground you route-find yourself. Use what is on either side as the test. The South Tahoma Glacier should fall away to climber's left and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to climber's right; if you find yourself on a glacier, or if the going out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you have drifted off the cleaver and are contouring around Pyramid Peak instead. Rockfall risk rises sharply with any party above you, the rock firms up above roughly 7,000 ft, and there are bivy sites around 8,100 to 8,300 ft.

waypoints.name: Rockfall chutes to Kautz Cleaver headwall
waypoints.note: Angle across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall and gain the Kautz Cleaver near 12,600 ft; helmet mandatory, best crossed before sun loosens rock.
waypoints.directions: Follow the cleaver crest up through class 3 and short class 4 rock bands and steep chutes, past bivy benches near 9,400 ft and the small col at about 10,700 ft. Higher, the crest holds a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow has melted off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies and across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall, joining the Kautz Cleaver between roughly 12,200 and 12,600 ft. Cross those chutes early, before the sun starts releasing rock and ice; helmets on.

waypoints.name: Point Success
waypoints.directions: From the Kautz Cleaver climb steepening snow and ice, generally around 45 degrees, to the headwall below the summit. A cliff band bars the way and is passed either by a short low fifth class rock step, exposed and sometimes wet or icy, or by an isolated snow and ice pitch of about 15 ft at up to 55 degrees, depending on the season. Above it the angle eases onto the summit plateau at Point Success, 14,158 ft.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin Pullout
waypoints.note: Large paved pullout at the hairpin turn on the North Cascades Highway just east of Washington Pass crest; no signed trailhead — find the boot path into the timber/boulder field on the uphill side. No parking pass is needed at this highway turnout.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the first hairpin turn about a mile east of the Washington Pass summit and park in the large paved turnout on the south side of the road, around 5,160 ft. Nothing here is signed as a trailhead; the boot path starts on the uphill side of the pullout, into the timber and boulders. SR-20 is gated for winter from roughly early December to mid or late April, so check the WSDOT pass report in the shoulder seasons. No parking pass is needed at this highway turnout.

waypoints.name: Boulder Field / Snowline
waypoints.note: Cairns mark the climbers' path up through timber and talus to about 5,800 ft, where the route commonly meets lingering snowpack well into summer.
waypoints.directions: From the pullout head south and southeast toward the foot of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch, below the north side of Kangaroo Temple. Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus and follow the cairns carefully: this lower boulder and talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach, and it is considerably worse when snow covers the tread early in the season. Around 5,800 ft you reach the level where snowpack commonly lingers well into summer.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Gain the crest of Kangaroo Ridge here between Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, about 1,500 ft above the trailhead; leave the approach path and turn east onto Wallaby's southwest ridge.
waypoints.directions: Above the boulder band the tread firms up into a distinct, easy-to-follow cairned trail through the upper basin. Keep climbing mixed talus, boulders and open slope to the crest of Kangaroo Ridge at Kangaroo Pass, 6,671 ft, roughly 1,500 ft of gain from the car in about 1 to 1.5 hours. A small tarn just below the pass is the only water on the route and can be dry by late summer or fall; there is none higher, so carry enough from the car. Expect snow on this stretch into early or mid summer depending on the year, and carry an ice axe or microspikes into July.

waypoints.name: 7,400 ft Ridge-to-Face Swing
waypoints.note: The southwest ridge narrows here; step off the crest and traverse onto the south-facing flank to reach the summit gully — boot tracks are sparse and easy to lose in poor visibility.
waypoints.directions: Leave the boot path at the pass and gain Wallaby's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail runs a short way and then disappears on rock, so the rest is route-finding: stay on or near the crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree and grassy benches, about 530 ft of gain to an access notch near 7,200 ft. The short section between that notch and about 7,400 ft is the technical crux of the route and holds a corniced snow arete into late spring, where an axe and light crampons are commonly used.

waypoints.name: South-Facing Summit Gully
waypoints.note: Loose talus and scree gully gains the final several hundred feet; Class 3 rock on either side avoids the worst scree, and this same gully is the descent line — watch for rockfall from parties above.
waypoints.directions: Where the crest narrows near 7,400 ft, step off it and traverse onto the south-facing flank to reach the summit gully. Boot tracks are sparse here and easy to lose in poor visibility. The gully is moderately steep with a great deal of loose rock and scree, so wear a helmet and avoid stacking the party directly above one another, since anyone higher will kick debris onto anyone below. Many parties take a short Class 3 line on the more solid rock at the gully's margins rather than wading up the scree.

waypoints.name: Wallaby Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Wallaby Peak on Kangaroo Ridge (7,995 ft); first climbed by Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney on June 17, 1942.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully for the final several hundred feet, then near its top exit left, to the northeast, for the short scramble to the true summit at 7,995 ft. The slabs just below the summit block stay exposed and are genuinely committing when wet or snow-covered, even in midsummer. This same gully is the descent line, downclimbed one at a time.

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard access point via FR-56/Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road; no day-use fee is currently charged at this specific trailhead (per USFS), though a free self-issue wilderness permit is required beyond it for Alpine Lakes Wilderness travel, and the road washout beyond this point means biking or hiking the closed roadbed toward Dutch Miller Gap.
waypoints.directions: FR-56 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to the lot is heavily potholed and rutted; parties in low-clearance cars routinely park short and walk the last stretch, which adds to an already long day.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Lake
waypoints.note: Standard high camp for the route, roughly 10 mi in via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail/old roadbed then a steep, unmaintained forested slog above a river ford near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trail; seldom-visited alpine lake below the Overcoat Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: The continuation of the road past the gate is roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed to Hardscrabble Horse Camp, and most parties bike it rather than walk it. Beyond that the Dutch Miller Gap Trail runs east along the north bank; the tread is reasonable but summer thimbleberry buries the rocks underfoot. Leave the trail about a mile before it swings toward Williams Lake and ford the river: it can run thigh-to-waist deep, and it is colder and higher on the way back than it was in the morning.

waypoints.name: Rock benches above Overcoat Glacier
waypoints.note: Higher alternate camp on open benches used to shorten summit day; this bivy option sits at roughly 6,600 ft.
waypoints.directions: Above the ford the ground climbs steeply through brush into a rocky corridor of waterfalls and steep faces before opening onto snow and benches. Snow lingers here well past midsummer. The awkward part is a sloping rock step partway up, which is markedly harder to downclimb than to climb and is worth noting for the return.

waypoints.name: Notch on Overcoat Peak's north ridge (Overcoat Col)
waypoints.note: Contour east from camp to this notch to gain the upper Overcoat Glacier; a col of the same name and elevation (~6,800 ft) sits beneath Chimney Rock's east face.
waypoints.directions: Only a couple of hundred feet of net gain, but it is a rising traverse over benches and old snow rather than a walk. The glacier starts immediately on the far side, so rope up and fit crampons at the notch rather than after stepping onto it.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the glacier's lower snowfields toward the snow finger below the east face; expect deep crevasses and weak, undermined snow bridges on this rapidly retreating glacier.
waypoints.directions: Drop onto the upper glacier from the notch and work toward the snow finger below the east face. Most parties time this route for the tail end of summer, when the crevasses are open and visible and the rock above is clear of snow; earlier in the season the bridges are the thing that will catch you out.

waypoints.name: Snow finger to east face
waypoints.note: Find the snow finger leading off the glacier onto the east face here, then pick up the Class 3-4 ledges and steep gully toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: The finger rises off the top of the glacier and is steep enough that crampons and a second tool are the norm. A crevasse commonly cuts it partway up and has to be turned. Near the dark towers at its top, move off snow onto rock and round the corner east to reach the ledge system.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; the final ~400 vertical ft is Class 4/low-5.0 ledges and a steep gully on the east side, with a small summit register.
waypoints.directions: The gully has solid holds but a few tall steps force committing, exposed moves, and most parties pitch it out on small cams and nuts in mediocre rock rather than soloing it. Sort the descent before you commit: the damp dihedral below is normally rappelled twice, not downclimbed.

waypoints.name: Snow Lakes Trailhead (Trail #1553)
waypoints.note: From Snow Lakes TH, hike Snow Lakes Trail #1553 up through Nada Lake/Snow Lakes and the Enchantment basin to Lake Viviane, where the crag sits directly alongside the trail.

waypoints.name: Snow Lakes
waypoints.note: Trail continues up past the lakes toward Enchantment Basin.

waypoints.name: Viviane Campsite (Lake Viviane)
waypoints.note: Reached after climbing ~6,400 vertical ft; limited campsites on either side of the lake outlet, adjacent to the crag.

waypoints.name: Base of Prusik Peak south face (approximate)
waypoints.note: Approximate — no reliable coordinate was found; the climbing zone is right at the base of Prusik Peak's south face/west ridge near the camp.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road's-end trailhead on Cascade River Road (23.1 mi gravel from Marblemount); NPS wilderness permit required for camps beyond Cascade Pass.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), about 23.1 miles of gravel road from Marblemount, at roughly 3,600 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here. Overnight parties also need a North Cascades backcountry camping permit for Kool-Aid Lake, picked up in person in Marblemount before you drive out.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail tops out here; leave it for the unmaintained climber's path bearing SSE toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: The Cascade Pass Trail is well-graded and heavily switchbacked the whole way, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft to the notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. It melts out by early to mid summer and is the busiest stretch of the trip, since it is a popular day hike in its own right. Nothing here needs route-finding; the work starts at the pass.

waypoints.name: Cache Glacier toe / Mixup Peak traverse
waypoints.note: Rising traverse on snow or heather across Mixup Peak's east flank to the base of Cache Glacier; isolated crevasses and firm morning snow can require an axe.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on Mixup Peak's east flank. The path is intermittent and vanishes entirely under early-season snow, so this is where navigation starts to matter. It brings you to the toe of the Cache Glacier around 6,000 ft, where firm morning snow makes an ice axe worth its weight.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Glaciated gap atop Cache Glacier between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak; descend SSE from here toward Kool-Aid Lake.
waypoints.directions: Ascend the glacier on moderate snow, steepening to about 35 degrees near the top, to reach the col. This glacier is small and generally free of significant crevasse hazard, but it is still a snow slope with runout below, so crampons are worth carrying depending on season and how firm it is.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn with established bivy sites used as base camp for the peak; outlet is snowbound and unreliable for water into early summer.
waypoints.directions: From the col the route drops rather than climbs: a climber's path makes a descending traverse to the southeast down to the lake. Do not continue north over the col. This is the last reliable water of the trip, and the outlet can still be snowbound into early summer, so fill here before going up.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain–Hurry-up Peak col
waypoints.note: Climb roughly 1,000 ft from Kool-Aid Lake to this saddle, then gain Magic Mountain's south ridge toward the false summit.
waypoints.directions: From the lake the ground turns up again onto heather and scree leading east to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, where the South Ridge proper begins. There is no water at all above the lake, so leave camp carrying what you need. The slope is uniform and featureless in cloud, which is the only real navigational catch on this leg.

waypoints.name: Corkscrew ledges below false summit
waypoints.note: Past the false summit, drop about 80 ft down a loose gully to exposed Class 3-4 ledges that corkscrew the east side of the peak; a hand line or short belay is often used here.
waypoints.directions: Follow the South Ridge up on heather and rock at class 3 to a false summit, roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true one. Do not try to stay on the crest from there. Drop about 50-80 ft down a loose, dirty gully on the far side to reach the ledge system, which is the technical crux of the whole outing.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit, marking the northern terminus of the Ptarmigan Traverse on the North Cascades NP / Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary.
waypoints.directions: The ledges are broken, exposed class 3-4 and corkscrew around the east side of the summit tower to the top. A hand line or a short belay is commonly used, and many parties rappel this section on the way down off a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there is no fixed hardware on this summit. Fresh snow can force a detour through the moat, and the loose rock means this section bites harder on the descent than on the way up.
